描述_ZN: Dhammapada" scroll, Ming, painted by Wu Bin, on paper with color, 118.8 cm in length and 53.1 cm in width.　　The picture depicts the story of Dharma, the first ancestor of Chinese Zen Buddhism, facing a wall and meditating. In the picture, Dharma has a dense beard, a fleshy bun on top of his head, and long earlobes, with the facial features of a Sanskrit monk, but his eyebrows and nose are not the deep eyes and high nose of the Westerners, but a blend of Chinese features. Dharma is dressed in red robes, with his right breast bare, sitting cross-legged on a futon. Dharma's face is meticulously carved, and the robe is clumsy and heavy, incorporating the brushwork of war brush and nail-headed rat's tail. The scene is simple, with a boulder standing diagonally behind Dharma, and the outline of the rock is lightly outlined with light ink, focusing on the texture of the rock with ink staining, and the ink color is deep and silent, blending with the mood of Dharma facing the wall and meditating.　　On the lower right side of this painting, the artist inscribed himself: "Written by Wu Bin Zhai, the Head of the Hidden Branch." Inscribed underneath are "Wu Bin's seal" in vermilion and "Wu Wenzhong's" in white. In the lower left corner are the seals of "Xie" in vermilion and "Aksobhya" in vermilion.　　Since the flourishing of Zen Buddhism in the Tang Dynasty, the six ancestors of Zen Buddhism have become popular subjects among literati and professional painters, with the most popular subjects being those representing Dharma facing the wall and crossing the river. Judging from the mark "written by Wu Bin Zaixin, the head of the branch hidden in the lower right corner of the painting, and the collection mark "offered by Aksobhya" in the lower left corner, this should be a work with an actual religious function. He advised Cheng Junji not to be influenced by pictures in his Zen practice from the perspective of Zen Buddhism's emphasis on the transmission of the heart, arguing that "to participate in a place without pictures is superior to others". Cao sol's postscript also illustrates from the opposite side the fact that at that time there existed "Zen with paintings".
